    SP --> BE
    SP2 --> BE
    CM --> BE
    BE --> TS

docs.title: Block 1: Data Connector
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-data-connector

Fetches raw data from any vendor and normalizes it into a MarketData object. Every connector wraps a different API but returns the same output.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient

data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"],
    start="2022-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

Available connectors: Yahoo Finance, Alpha Vantage, Finnhub, EOD Historical Data.

docs.title: Block 2: MarketData
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-core

MarketData is the universal data container passed between all blocks. It holds:

Field Type Description prices pd.DataFrame Daily closing prices (rows = dates, cols = assets) features dict[str, pd.DataFrame] Time-series features: volume, macro, technicals, etc. cross_sectional pd.DataFrame \| None Market caps, sector mappings, etc. risk_free_rate pd.Series \| float Constant or time-varying risk-free rate risk_aversion pd.Series \| float 0 = most aggressive, 1 = most conservative

Zero-Lookahead Guarantee

MarketData.validate_alignment() raises an error if any feature index doesn't perfectly align with the price index. MarketData.slice_time(end_date, lookback) creates a safe time-window slice for each backtest period, preventing future data from leaking into the estimation window.

docs.title: Block 3: Return Estimator
docs.text:
Interface: BaseReturnEstimator.estimate(data: MarketData) -> pd.Series

Produces a pd.Series of annualized expected returns, one per asset. Plug any estimator into StrategyPipeline.

Estimator When to use EWMAReturnEstimator Recent returns matter more (default) MomentumReturnEstimator Cross-sectional momentum signal FactorReturnEstimator Factor-model attribution (Fama-French style) JamesSteinReturnEstimator Shrinkage — great for large asset universes ImpliedReturnEstimator Reverse-optimization from known market weights BlackLittermanEstimator Blend market equilibrium with investor views

docs.title: Block 4: Covariance Estimator
docs.text:
Interface: BaseCovarianceEstimator.estimate(data: MarketData) -> pd.DataFrame

Produces an NxN covariance matrix. The choice of estimator significantly affects optimizer stability.

Estimator When to use EmpiricalCovariance Large T/N ratio, stable markets EWMACovariance Recent volatility clusters matter LedoitWolfEstimator Small sample, high-dimensional portfolios RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator Remove noise eigenvalues, detect true factors SemiCovariance Focus on downside risk only

docs.title: Block 5: Allocator
docs.text:
Interface: BaseAllocator.allocate(data, cov_matrix, expected_returns) -> OptimizationResult

Solves for optimal portfolio weights given the estimated inputs.

Classical (convex optimization via CVXPY):

Allocator Requires returns? EqualWeightAllocator No MarkowitzAllocator For Max Sharpe / Max Return RiskParityAllocator No RiskBudgetingAllocator No (uses data.features["risk_budgets"]) MaxDiversificationAllocator No

Graph-based ML (hierarchical clustering, no matrix inversion):

Allocator Method HRPAllocator Hierarchical Risk Parity HERCAllocator Hierarchical Equal Risk Contribution NCOAllocator Nested Cluster Optimization

docs.title: Block 6: StrategyPipeline
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-core

StrategyPipeline is the glue that connects your estimators and allocator into a single callable unit. The backtest engine only knows about StrategyPipeline — it doesn't care which estimator or allocator you've chosen.

from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MyAllocator(tickers=...),
    returns_estimator=MyReturnEstimator(),   # optional, defaults to EWMA
    cov_estimator=MyCovarianceEstimator(),   # optional, defaults to Empirical
)

weights = pipeline.generate_weights(data)  # → pd.Series

docs.title: Block 7: WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-backtest

The engine runs your StrategyPipeline across rolling or expanding historical windows, applying transaction costs on each rebalance. It enforces the zero-lookahead guarantee by slicing MarketData before each pipeline call.

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",                  # monthly
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(252),  # 1-year lookback
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(10.0),    # 10bps per trade
)

results = engine.run(data)
# → {"returns": pd.Series, "weights": pd.DataFrame, "tear_sheet": pd.DataFrame}

docs.title: Block 8: Monte Carlo Simulation & Entropy Pooling
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-simulation & pyalloq-core

Generates 3D \((M, T, N)\) synthetic price and feature tensors (ScenarioMarketData), blends non-Gaussian return and volatility views via EntropyPooler, and executes WalkForwardEngine across all \(M\) paths in parallel via ParallelMonteCarloEngine.

from pyalloq_simulation import GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator
from pyalloq_core.engines import ParallelMonteCarloEngine

gen = GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator(nu=5.0)
gen.fit(data)

mc_engine = ParallelMonteCarloEngine(backtest_engine=engine, max_workers=4)
mc_result = mc_engine.run_batches(gen.generate_batches(n_paths=500, horizon=252, batch_size=100))

docs.title: How They Fit Together
docs.text:
Every portfolio optimization workflow in PyAlloq follows the same linear data flow:

Data Connector → MarketData → [Return Estimator + Covariance Estimator] → Allocator
                                         ↕ (via StrategyPipeline)
                              WalkForwardEngine [+ Splitter + Cost Model]
                                         ↓
                                     TearSheet

This separation of concerns means you can:

  • Change the data source without touching your estimators
  • Change estimators without touching your allocator
  • Change the allocator without touching the backtest engine
  • Change cost models or splitters without changing anything else

docs.title: MarketData
docs.text:
MarketData is the single source of truth for all financial data in PyAlloq. Every building block — estimators, allocators, the backtest engine — consumes and produces MarketData.

Understanding how it works is essential to avoiding look-ahead bias in backtesting.

docs.title: Data Fields
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,                    # required: (T × N) closing prices
    features={"volume": volume_df},      # optional: time-series features
    cross_sectional=market_caps_df,      # optional: static cross-sectional data
    risk_free_rate=0.04,                 # constant or pd.Series
    risk_aversion=1.0,                   # 0 = aggressive, 1 = conservative
)
Field Type Required Description prices pd.DataFrame ✅ Closing prices. Rows = dates, Columns = ticker symbols assets list[str] Auto Auto-inferred from prices.columns if not provided features dict[str, pd.DataFrame] ❌ Named time-series feature matrices. Must share the same DatetimeIndex as prices cross_sectional pd.DataFrame \| None ❌ Cross-sectional data (e.g., market caps, sector labels). Not time-indexed risk_free_rate pd.Series \| float ❌ Annual risk-free rate. Defaults to 0.0 risk_aversion pd.Series \| float ❌ Used by MarkowitzAllocator for MAX_RETURN utility. Defaults to 1.0

docs.title: The Features Dictionary
docs.text:
features is a flexible dictionary of named pd.DataFrame matrices. Use it to attach any time-series signal to your market data:

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={
        "volume":        volume_df,           # daily traded volume
        "momentum_12m":  momentum_df,         # 12-month momentum signals
        "risk_budgets":  risk_budget_df,      # per-asset risk budgets (for RiskBudgetingAllocator)
        "vix":           vix_df,              # macro features
    }
)

Risk Budgets

RiskBudgetingAllocator reads its target budgets from data.features["risk_budgets"]. This is the standard way to pass allocator-specific inputs through the pipeline.

Almgren-Chriss Cost Model

AlmgrenChrissCostModel requires data.features["volume"] to be set for calculating market impact costs.

docs.title: validate_alignment()
docs.text:
Called automatically at construction time. Raises a ValueError if any feature matrix's index does not exactly match prices.index. This prevents silent data misalignment bugs.

# This raises ValueError immediately — catching the bug at construction, not later
data = MarketData(
    prices=daily_prices,
    features={"macro": weekly_macro_df},  # ❌ weekly index ≠ daily index
)
# ValueError: Data misalignment: Feature: macro index does not perfectly match 'prices' index.

docs.title: slice_time(end_date, lookback)
docs.text:
Creates a new MarketData instance safely sliced up to (and including) end_date. The backtest engine calls this for every rebalance window.

# Inside WalkForwardEngine — what happens at each rebalance date:
window_data = data.slice_time(
    end_date=pd.Timestamp("2023-06-30"),
    lookback=252,  # use 1 year of history
)

# window_data.prices ends at 2023-06-30 — no future data leaks through
weights = pipeline.generate_weights(window_data)

slice_time slices all fields consistently: prices, all features, and risk_free_rate (if a Series). The cross_sectional field is passed through unchanged since it is not time-indexed.

docs.title: Working with MarketData Directly
docs.text:
You can generate returns from prices:

returns = data.prices.pct_change().dropna()

Or select a sub-universe:

us_data = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices[["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"]],
    risk_free_rate=data.risk_free_rate,
)

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
MarketData is intentionally a dumb container, not a class with business logic. This design choice means:

  • All components receive the same type of input
  • There is one canonical data format — no per-component data munging
  • Time alignment is validated once at construction, not repeatedly inside each component
  • The backtest engine can slice the data safely without knowing what's inside it

docs.title: ScenarioMarketData (3D Synthetic Tensors)
docs.text:
For Monte Carlo simulation (pyalloq-simulation), ScenarioMarketData wraps 3D \((M, T, N)\) synthetic price, return, and exogenous feature tensors while providing a zero-copy bridge back to 2D MarketData per path:

from pyalloq_core.data import ScenarioMarketData

# Slice path m into a standard 2D MarketData instance compatible with WalkForwardEngine
path_data = scenario_data.get_path(path_idx=0, feature_pipeline=my_feature_pipeline)

# Compute full-horizon cumulative asset returns (M × N) anchored at t=0 initial_prices
cum_returns = scenario_data.get_cumulative_returns()
Field Type Shape Description prices np.ndarray (M, T, N) Simulated asset price paths returns np.ndarray (M, T, N) Simulated single-step asset returns asset_names list[str] (N,) Ordered ticker symbols initial_prices np.ndarray \| None (N,) \(t=0\) anchor prices from the end of historical data timestamps pd.Index (T,) Forward-projected DatetimeIndex (or RangeIndex) features dict[str, np.ndarray] (M, T, K) Jointly synthesized exogenous feature tensors

docs.title: Swapping Components
docs.text:
Because every component in PyAlloq implements a clean interface, you can swap any piece of the stack with a single line of code — without changing anything else.

This page shows side-by-side examples of the most common swaps.

docs.title: Swapping Covariance Estimators
docs.text:
The covariance estimator has the biggest impact on optimizer stability, especially for Markowitz-family allocators. Try each with the same pipeline and compare results.

Empirical (Default)Ledoit-Wolf ShrinkageRMT DenoisingSemi-Covariance 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.empirical import EmpiricalCovariance
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=EmpiricalCovariance(),  # sample covariance — sensitive to outliers
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),  # analytically optimal shrinkage intensity
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.random_matrix_theory import RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator(denoise=True, detone=False),
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.semi_covariance import SemiCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=SemiCovariance(),  # penalizes downside volatility only
)

docs.title: Swapping Return Estimators
docs.text:
For allocators that use expected returns (Max Sharpe, Max Return, Black-Litterman), the choice of return estimator directly impacts weights.

EWMA (Default)James-Stein ShrinkageVolatility-Scaled MomentumResidual MomentumTimesFM 3.0 (Foundation Model)Implied Returns 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.ewma import EWMAReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=EWMAReturnEstimator(),  # exponentially weighted mean
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),  # shrinks towards grand mean
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator(),  # multi-horizon volatility-scaled z-score
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import ResidualMomentumEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=ResidualMomentumEstimator(),  # beta-neutralized idiosyncratic momentum
)

from pyalloq.dl.estimators.returns.timesfm import TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

tfm_model = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)  # Loaded TimesFM 3.0 evaluator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator(model=tfm_model, horizon=21),
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.implied import ImpliedReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=ImpliedReturnEstimator(),  # reverse-optimization from market weights
)

docs.title: Swapping Allocators
docs.text:
The allocator is completely decoupled from estimators and the backtest engine. Swap it freely.

Risk ParityMarkowitz (Min Vol)HRP (Hierarchical Risk Parity)Max DiversificationEqual Weight (Baseline) 
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
)

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
)

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
)

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.max_diversification import MaxDiversificationAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MaxDiversificationAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
)

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.naive import EqualWeightAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
)

docs.title: Swapping Backtest Splitters
docs.text:
The splitter controls how the engine partitions history for each rebalance window. Swap it in WalkForwardEngine.

Rolling Window (Default)Expanding Window 
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=252),  # fixed 1-year window
)

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252),  # grows with all available history
)

docs.title: Swapping Transaction Cost Models
docs.text:
Flat Bps (Default)Almgren-Chriss Market Impact 
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import FlatBpsCostModel

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0),  # 10 basis points per trade
)

from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

# Requires data.features["volume"] to be set
engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    cost_model=AlmgrenChrissCostModel(
        portfolio_aum=1_000_000,
        spread_bps=2.0,
        gamma=0.1,
    ),
)

docs.title: Comparing Strategies Side-by-Side
docs.text:
Run multiple pipelines through the same engine and collect results for comparison:

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

strategies = {
    "Equal Weight":   EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "Risk Parity":    RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "HRP":            HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "Min Volatility": MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
}

results = {}
for name, allocator in strategies.items():
    pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=allocator)
    engine = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline, rebalance_freq="ME")
    results[name] = engine.run(data)

# Compare Sharpe ratios
for name, res in results.items():
    sharpe = res["tear_sheet"].loc["sharpe_ratio", "Value"]
    print(f"{name:<20} Sharpe: {sharpe:.2f}")

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: PyAlloq requires Python 3.11+.

docs.title: Using uv (Recommended)
docs.text:
uv is the recommended package manager for PyAlloq.

uv add pyalloq

To also install optional machine learning or deep learning extras:

# Deep learning (PyTorch-based models)
uv add "pyalloq[dl]"

# Reinforcement learning (Stable-Baselines3 + Gymnasium)
uv add "pyalloq[rl]"

# All ML extras
uv add "pyalloq[all-ml]"

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text:
pip install pyalloq

With optional extras:

pip install "pyalloq[dl]"
pip install "pyalloq[rl]"
pip install "pyalloq[all-ml]"

docs.title: Development Installation (from source)
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install all workspace packages together:

git clone https://github.com/AlloqAlpha/pyalloq.git
cd pyalloq

# Install all workspace packages + dev dependencies
uv sync --all-extras

This installs pyalloq, pyalloq-core, pyalloq-backtest, pyalloq-data-connector, pyalloq-features, pyalloq-simulation, and pyalloq-viz as editable workspace packages.

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text: Extra Key packages Use case [dl] torch>=2.0 Deep learning return/covariance estimators [rl] stable-baselines3, gymnasium Reinforcement learning allocators [all-ml] All of the above Full ML stack

docs.text:
import pyalloq
import pyalloq_core
import pyalloq_backtest
import pyalloq_data_connector
import pyalloq_simulation
import pyalloq_viz

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This guide walks you through building and backtesting a complete portfolio strategy end-to-end.

docs.title: Step 1 — Fetch Market Data
docs.text:
Use a data connector to download prices. All connectors return a standardized MarketData object.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient

client = YahooFinanceClient()
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN", "TSLA"],
    start="2020-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

print(data.assets)   # ['AAPL', 'MSFT', 'GOOGL', 'AMZN', 'TSLA']
print(data.prices.shape)  # (1006, 5)

docs.title: Step 2 — Choose an Allocator
docs.text:
Pick any allocator from pyalloq.classical.optimizers or pyalloq.ml.optimizers. Every allocator implements the same BaseAllocator interface.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

allocator = RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)

docs.title: Step 3 — Build a Strategy Pipeline
docs.text:
StrategyPipeline wires together your return estimator, covariance estimator, and allocator. Defaults are EWMA returns and empirical covariance.

from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=allocator)

To customize the estimators:

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

docs.title: Step 4 — Run a Walk-Forward Backtest
docs.text:
WalkForwardEngine runs your pipeline on rolling windows of historical data, rebalancing at a specified frequency, and accounts for transaction costs.

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",  # Monthly rebalancing
)

results = engine.run(data)

docs.title: Step 5 — Inspect Results
docs.text:
The engine returns a dictionary with portfolio returns, daily weights, and a performance tear sheet.

print(results["tear_sheet"])

                       Value
total_return            1.23
annualized_return       0.21
annualized_volatility   0.14
sharpe_ratio            1.45
maximum_drawdown       -0.18
calmar_ratio            1.17

You can also access the raw returns and weight history:

portfolio_returns = results["returns"]     # pd.Series
weight_history    = results["weights"]     # pd.DataFrame

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

# 1. Fetch data
data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN", "TSLA"],
    start="2020-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

# 2. Build pipeline
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

# 3. Run backtest
results = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline, rebalance_freq="ME").run(data)

# 4. Review performance
print(results["tear_sheet"])

docs.title: Estimator Mathematics
docs.text: This page covers the mathematical foundations of the return and covariance estimators implemented in pyalloq.

docs.title: Exponentially Weighted Mean (EWMA)
docs.text:
Weights observations exponentially so that recent returns matter more:

\[ \hat{\mu}^{EWMA}_i = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda^{T-t} r_{i,t}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda^{T-t}} \]

where the decay factor \(\lambda = 1 - \frac{2}{\text{span}+1}\).

docs.title: James-Stein Shrinkage
docs.text:
Shrinks each asset's historical mean towards the grand mean of all assets. For \(N \geq 3\) assets, the James-Stein estimator strictly dominates the sample mean in terms of MSE:

\[ \hat{\mu}^{JS} = (1 - w^*) \hat{\mu} + w^* \bar{\mu} \mathbf{1} \]

The optimal shrinkage intensity \(w^*\) is:

\[ w^* = \min\left(1,\; \frac{N-2}{(\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})^\top \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} (\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})}\right) \]

where \(\bar{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \hat{\mu}_i\) is the grand mean.

docs.title: Implied Returns (Reverse Optimization)
docs.text:
Given observed market-capitalization weights \(w^{mkt}\) and the market risk aversion \(\lambda\), the implied equilibrium excess returns are:

\[ \Pi = \lambda \Sigma w^{mkt} \]

This is the equilibrium prior used in Black-Litterman.

docs.title: Black-Litterman
docs.text:
Combines the market equilibrium prior \(\Pi\) with investor views \((P, Q)\) through Bayesian updating.

Views: \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}\) is a view-picking matrix, \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^K\) are the expected view returns, and \(\Omega\) is the uncertainty matrix for the views.

Posterior expected returns:

\[ \mu^* = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} \Pi + P^\top \Omega^{-1} Q\right] \]

Posterior covariance:

\[ \Sigma^* = \Sigma + \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \]

where \(\tau\) is a scalar controlling the uncertainty in the prior (typically 0.01–0.05).

docs.title: Ledoit-Wolf Shrinkage
docs.text:
Shrinks the sample covariance \(\hat{\Sigma}\) towards a structured target \(T\) (e.g., diagonal matrix):

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^*) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^* \hat{\mu}_{cov} I \]

The optimal shrinkage intensity \(\alpha^*\) is derived analytically by minimizing the Frobenius norm of the estimation error:

\[ \alpha^* = \frac{\delta^2}{\gamma^2} \]

where \(\delta^2\) and \(\gamma^2\) are data-dependent scaling constants derived from the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) method.

See: Ledoit & Wolf (2004)

docs.title: Random Matrix Theory (Marchenko-Pastur)
docs.text:
For a random matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N}\) with i.i.d. entries, the eigenvalue distribution of \(\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T} X^\top X\) converges to the Marchenko-Pastur distribution with upper bound:

\[ \lambda_+ = \sigma^2 \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{T}}\right)^2 \]

Any empirical eigenvalue \(\lambda_i < \lambda_+\) is attributable to noise, not signal. The denoising step replaces these with the average noise eigenvalue:

\[ \bar{\lambda}_{noise} = \frac{\sum_{i: \lambda_i < \lambda_+} \lambda_i}{|\{i: \lambda_i < \lambda_+\}|} \]

Then the clean covariance is reconstructed: \(\hat{\Sigma}^{RMT} = V \Lambda_{clean} V^\top\)

The optional detoning step removes the largest eigenvalue (corresponding to the market-wide factor) from the correlation matrix before reconstruction, isolating sector-level correlations.

docs.title: Semi-Covariance
docs.text:
Uses only negative return periods to estimate covariance, focusing on downside co-movement:

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{semi}_{ij} = \frac{1}{T^-} \sum_{t: r_{i,t} < 0} r_{i,t} \cdot r_{j,t} \]

where \(T^-\) is the count of periods where asset \(i\) had a negative return.

docs.title: EWMA Covariance
docs.text:
Uses exponential weighting to capture time-varying covariance:

\[ \hat{\Sigma}_t = (1 - \lambda) r_t r_t^\top + \lambda \hat{\Sigma}_{t-1} \]

where \(\lambda = 1 - \frac{2}{\text{span}+1}\) is the decay factor. This models volatility clustering observed in financial time series (similar to the RiskMetrics model).

docs.title: Graph-Based Allocator Mathematics
docs.text:
This page covers the mathematical foundations of the hierarchical clustering-based allocators: HRP, HERC, and NCO.

These methods avoid inverting the covariance matrix, making them more numerically stable for large universes and ill-conditioned matrices.

docs.title: Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP)
docs.text: López de Prado (2016). HRP uses hierarchical clustering on the correlation matrix to build a tree of related assets, then allocates weights top-down through the tree using inverse-variance weighting.

docs.title: Step 1: Distance Matrix
docs.text:
Convert the correlation matrix \(\rho\) into a metric distance matrix:

\[ d_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho_{ij}}{2}} \]

Properties: \(d_{ii} = 0\), \(d_{ij} = d_{ji}\), \(0 \leq d_{ij} \leq 1\).

docs.title: Step 2: Hierarchical Clustering (Dendrogram)
docs.text:
Apply single-linkage agglomerative clustering to the distance matrix to build a binary tree (dendrogram). At each merge step, the distance between two clusters is:

\[ d(C_1, C_2) = \min_{i \in C_1, j \in C_2} d_{ij} \]

docs.title: Step 3: Quasi-Diagonalization
docs.text: Re-order the assets (leaves of the dendrogram) such that similar assets are adjacent. The resulting reordering makes the covariance matrix approximately block-diagonal.

docs.title: Step 4: Recursive Bisection
docs.text:
Traverse the dendrogram top-down. At each level, split the current cluster into two sub-clusters and allocate capital inversely proportional to their sub-portfolio variances:

\[ w_{left} \leftarrow w_{left} \times \alpha, \quad w_{right} \leftarrow w_{right} \times (1 - \alpha) \]

where the allocation split \(\alpha\) is:

\[ \alpha = 1 - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}^2_{left}}{\tilde{\sigma}^2_{left} + \tilde{\sigma}^2_{right}} \]

and \(\tilde{\sigma}^2_C\) is the variance of the inverse-variance portfolio of cluster \(C\):

\[ \tilde{w}_i = \frac{1/\sigma^2_i}{\sum_{j \in C} 1/\sigma^2_j}, \quad \tilde{\sigma}^2_C = \tilde{w}^\top_C \Sigma_C \tilde{w}_C \]

docs.title: Hierarchical Equal Risk Contribution (HERC)
docs.text:
HERC extends HRP by replacing the inverse-variance cluster weights at each bisection step with equal risk contribution weights within each cluster. This enforces risk parity not just at the asset level but at every level of the hierarchy.

At each cluster node, the intra-cluster weights are the ERC solution:

\[ \min_{y_C \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y_C^\top \Sigma_C y_C - \sum_{i \in C} \ln y_{C,i} \]

The inter-cluster allocation still follows the same recursive bisection as HRP, but using the ERC cluster variance instead of the IVP cluster variance.

docs.title: Nested Cluster Optimization (NCO)
docs.text: López de Prado (2019). NCO applies two-level Markowitz optimization:

docs.title: Step 1: Cluster Detection
docs.text: Apply k-means clustering to the correlation matrix (using the first \(k\) principal components as cluster features) to partition assets into \(K\) clusters.

docs.title: Step 2: Intra-Cluster Optimization
docs.text:
Run a within-cluster Markowitz optimization for each cluster \(C_k\) independently:

\[ w^{intra}_{C_k} = \arg\min_{w \geq 0} w^\top \Sigma_{C_k} w \]

This produces one synthetic "cluster portfolio" per cluster.

docs.title: Step 3: Inter-Cluster Optimization
docs.text:
Build a reduced \(K \times K\) covariance matrix from the cluster portfolio returns, and run a second Markowitz optimization across cluster representatives:

\[ w^{inter} = \arg\min_{u \geq 0} u^\top \Sigma^{cluster} u \]

docs.title: Step 4: Combine
docs.text:
The final weight for asset \(i\) in cluster \(C_k\) is:

\[ w_i = w^{intra}_{i \in C_k} \times w^{inter}_{C_k} \]

docs.text: Property HRP HERC NCO Matrix inversion ❌ ❌ ✅ (within clusters only) Risk budget control Implicit (IVP) Explicit (ERC) Implicit (MinVol) Cluster method Hierarchical linkage Hierarchical linkage K-Means Complexity Low Medium Higher Large universe (100+) ✅ ✅ ✅

docs.title: Monte Carlo & Entropy Pooling Mathematics
docs.text: This page covers the mathematical foundations of the scenario generators, missing-history imputation, Meucci's Entropy Pooling (first- and second-moment views), and path-dependent risk metrics implemented in pyalloq-simulation.

docs.title: 1. PCA Factor Back-Casting Imputation
docs.text:
When asset \(j\) has missing historical observations (e.g., a recent IPO missing \(t \in \mathcal{M}_j\) and observed on \(t \in \mathcal{O}_j\)), FactorBackcastImputer avoids truncating the \(N\)-asset matrix:

  1. Identify anchor assets \(\mathcal{A}\) with coverage \(\ge c_{\min}\) and extract \(K\) orthogonal latent factor series \(F \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times K}\) via Principal Component Analysis on anchor returns.
  2. Estimate ridge-stabilized factor loadings for asset \(j\) on its observed window \(\mathcal{O}_j\):
\[ \hat{\beta}_j = \left(X_{\mathcal{O}_j}^\top X_{\mathcal{O}_j} + \lambda I\right)^{-1} X_{\mathcal{O}_j}^\top r_{j, \mathcal{O}_j}, \quad X_t = [1, F_t] \]
  1. Impute missing returns for \(t \in \mathcal{M}_j\) with matched idiosyncratic residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}_{\epsilon, j}^2\):
\[ \hat{r}_{j, t} = X_t \hat{\beta}_j + \epsilon_{j, t}, \quad \epsilon_{j, t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \hat{\sigma}_{\epsilon, j}^2) \]
  1. Back-cast pre-IPO prices recursively from the first observed price \(P_{j, t_0}\):
\[ P_{j, t} = \frac{P_{j, t+1}}{1 + \hat{r}_{j, t+1}}, \quad t = t_0 - 1, \dots, 0 \]

docs.title: Filtered Historical Simulation (FHSGenerator)
docs.text:
Filtered Historical Simulation (Barone-Adesi et al., 1999) strips volatility clustering using univariate GARCH(1,1) models while preserving empirical cross-asset dependence and fat tails via non-parametric residual bootstrapping:

\[ r_{i, t} = \mu_i + \epsilon_{i, t}, \quad \epsilon_{i, t} = \sigma_{i, t} z_{i, t} \] \[ \sigma_{i, t}^2 = \omega_i + \alpha_i \epsilon_{i, t-1}^2 + \beta_i \sigma_{i, t-1}^2 \]

At each simulated step \(t\), a random historical date index \(\tau \sim \text{Uniform}\{1, \dots, T_{\text{hist}}\}\) is drawn synchronously across all \(N\) assets, preserving cross-sectional co-movement \(Z_{\tau} = (\hat{z}_{1, \tau}, \dots, \hat{z}_{N, \tau})\).

docs.title: GARCH-EVT-Student-\(t\) Copula (GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator)
docs.text:
To model extreme tail risk and positive lower-tail dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)), GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator combines AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) filtration with Extreme Value Theory (McNeil & Frey, 2000) and a Student-\(t\) Copula:

  1. AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) Filtration: Extracts standardized residuals \(z_{i, t} = \epsilon_{i, t} / \sigma_{i, t}\).
  2. Semi-Parametric Generalized Pareto (GPD) Marginals: Given lower and upper quantile thresholds \(u_L, u_U\) at probabilities \(q_L, q_U\), exceedances in the tails follow the Generalized Pareto Distribution:
\[ F_i(z) = egin{cases} q_L \left(1 - G_{\xi_{L,i}, eta_{L,i}}(u_L - z) ight) & z < u_L \ \hat{F}_{ ext{emp}}(z) & u_L \le z \le u_U \ q_U + (1 - q_U) G_{\xi_{U,i}, eta_{U,i}}(z - u_U) & z > u_U \end{cases} \]

where the GPD cumulative distribution function is:

\[ G_{\xi, eta}(y) = 1 - \left(1 + rac{\xi y}{ eta} ight)^{-1/\xi} \]
  1. Student-\(t\) Copula Binding: Uniform marginals \(u_{i, t} = F_i(z_{i, t})\) are mapped via the univariate Student-\(t\) quantile \(t_ u^{-1}(u_{i, t})\) to estimate the copula correlation matrix \(R\) with degrees of freedom \( u\). Lower-tail dependence between assets \(i\) and \(j\) is strictly positive:
\[ \lambda_L = 2 \, t_{ u + 1}\!\left(-\sqrt{ rac{( u + 1)(1 - ho_{ij})}{1 + ho_{ij}}} ight) > 0 \]

docs.title: Gaussian Mixture Markov Regimes (GMMRegimeGenerator)
docs.text:
Models discrete latent market states \(s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) via a \(K\)-component Gaussian Mixture Model:

\[ p(r_t) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(r_t \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k) \]

Historical states are decoded via maximum a posteriori assignment \(\hat{s}_t = \arg\max_k \gamma_{t, k}\), yielding the empirical Markov transition matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K}\) with entries \(P_{ab} = \mathbb{P}(s_{t} = b \mid s_{t-1} = a)\). Forward paths evolve \(s_{m, t} \sim P_{s_{m, t-1}, \cdot}\) and draw \(r_{m, t} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{s_{m, t}}, \Sigma_{s_{m, t}})\).

docs.title: 3. Meucci's Entropy Pooling (EntropyPooler & ViewBuilder)
docs.text:
Given \(M\) simulated scenarios with prior probability vector \(p \in \Delta^M\) (typically uniform \(p_m = 1/M\)), Entropy Pooling (Meucci, 2008) finds the posterior probability distribution \(x \in \Delta^M\) that satisfies linear equality and inequality views while minimizing Relative Entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence):

\[ \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^M} \mathcal{E}(x \,\|\, p) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} x_m \ln\!\left(\frac{x_m}{p_m}\right) \]

subject to:

\[ A x \le b, \quad C x = d, \quad \mathbf{1}^\top x = 1, \quad x \ge 0 \]

docs.title: Unconstrained Dual Formulation
docs.text:
Rather than solving an \(M\)-dimensional primal problem (\(M \sim 10,000\)), EntropyPooler solves the low-dimensional Lagrange dual over the \(V\) view multipliers \(\gamma = (\lambda, u)\) where \( u \ge 0\):

\[ \min_{\lambda, u \ge 0} \; \ln\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M p_m \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma]_m ight) ight) + \gamma^ op ext{targets}, \quad G = egin{bmatrix} C \ A \end{bmatrix} \]

The posterior scenario weights are recovered analytically via the log-sum-exp stabilized Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution:

\[ x^*_m = rac{p_m \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma^*]_m ight)}{\sum_{k=1}^M p_k \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma^*]_k ight)} \]

docs.title: First- and Second-Moment View Linearization
docs.text:
Because expectation under the scenario measure is a linear inner product \(\mathbb{E}_x[g(R)] = \sum_{m=1}^M x_m g(R_m)\), both first- and second-moment views are linear in the probability vector \(x\):

Absolute Return View (AbsoluteView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m R_{m, i} \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \mu_i^{\text{target}} \]

Relative Return View (RelativeView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - R_{m, j}) \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \delta_{ij}^{\text{target}} \]

Volatility View (VolatilityView) — centered around the reference mean \(\bar{\mu}_i\):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - \bar{\mu}_i)^2 \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \left(\sigma_i^{\text{target}}\right)^2 \]

Covariance / Correlation View (CovarianceView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - \bar{\mu}_i)(R_{m, j} - \bar{\mu}_j) \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \rho_{ij}^{\text{target}} \bar{\sigma}_i \bar{\sigma}_j \]

docs.title: 4. Path-Dependent Risk Metrics (ScenarioEvaluator)
docs.text:
Let \(W_{m, t}\) denote the simulated portfolio wealth on path \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) at time step \(t \in \{0, \dots, T\}\) with \(W_{m, 0} = 1\):

Path Maximum Drawdown (\(\text{MDD}_m\)):

\[ \text{MDD}_m = \min_{0 \le t \le T} \frac{W_{m, t} - \max_{0 \le \tau \le t} W_{m, \tau}}{\max_{0 \le \tau \le t} W_{m, \tau}} \le 0 \]

View-Adjusted Maximum Drawdown:

\[ \text{MDD}_{\text{view}} = \sum_{m=1}^M x^*_m \, \text{MDD}_m \]

Probability of Ruin (\(\mathbb{P}_{\text{ruin}}\)) — for critical drawdown threshold \(\theta_{\text{ruin}} < 0\) (e.g., \(-0.30\)):

\[ \mathbb{P}_{\text{ruin}}(\theta_{\text{ruin}}) = \sum_{m=1}^M x^*_m \, \mathbb{I}\!\left(\text{MDD}_m \le \theta_{\text{ruin}}\right) \]

docs.title: Combinatorial Symmetric Cross-Validation (PBOEvaluator)
docs.text:
Given a return matrix \(M_{\text{trials}} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times M}\) of \(M\) candidate strategy configurations evaluated over \(T\) observations, CSCV (Bailey et al., 2017) partitions time into \(S\) even submatrices and forms all \(C = \binom{S}{S/2}\) training (In-Sample, \(J\)) and testing (Out-of-Sample, \(\bar{J}\)) combinations:

  1. For each split \(c \in \{1, \dots, C\}\), compute the vector of In-Sample Sharpe ratios \(R_c \in \mathbb{R}^M\) on \(J_c\) and Out-of-Sample Sharpe ratios \(\bar{R}_c \in \mathbb{R}^M\) on \(\bar{J}_c\).
  2. Select the In-Sample optimal strategy \(m^* = \arg\max_m R_{c, m}\) and find its relative rank \(\omega_c \in (0, 1)\) within the Out-of-Sample distribution \(\bar{R}_c\).
  3. Define the Rank Logit \(\lambda_c\):
\[ \lambda_c = \ln\!\left(\frac{\omega_c}{1 - \omega_c}\right) \]

When \(\lambda_c \le 0\), the strategy selected as best In-Sample performs worse than the median strategy Out-of-Sample. The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) is the empirical probability mass in the left tail:

\[ \text{PBO} = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^C \mathbb{I}\!\left(\lambda_c \le 0\right) \]

docs.title: Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCVSplitter)
docs.text: Given \(N\) chronological groups and \(k\) test groups per split, there are \(\binom{N}{k}\) train/test splits with purge window \(p\) and embargo window \(e\) applied around every test block boundary. Because each group appears in exactly \(\varphi(N, k) = \binom{N - 1}{k - 1}\) test sets across all splits, the out-of-sample predictions can be reassembled into \(\varphi(N, k)\) full-horizon backtest paths rather than a single point estimate (López de Prado, 2018).

docs.title: Portfolio Theory
docs.text: This page documents the mathematical formulations behind each classical allocator implemented in pyalloq.

docs.title: Markowitz Mean-Variance Optimization
docs.text: Markowitz (1952) introduced the canonical portfolio optimization framework: find the weights \(w\) that minimize portfolio variance for a given level of expected return.

docs.title: Minimum Variance
docs.text:
\[ \min_{w} \; w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1, \quad w \geq 0 \]

where \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) is the covariance matrix of asset returns.

docs.title: Maximum Sharpe Ratio
docs.text:
Directly maximizing the Sharpe ratio is non-convex. Tobin's mutual fund separation theorem allows the problem to be recast as a convex quadratic program via the substitution trick:

Let \(y = \kappa w\) where \(\kappa = \frac{1}{(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top w}\). Then:

\[ \max_{w} \; \frac{(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top w}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \;\equiv\; \min_{y} \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top y = 1, \quad y \geq 0 \]

Recover weights: \(w^* = y^* / \mathbf{1}^\top y^*\)

docs.title: Maximum Utility (Mean-Variance)
docs.text:
Maximize the mean-variance utility function with a risk aversion parameter \(\lambda\):

\[ \max_{w} \; \mu^\top w - \lambda \cdot w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1, \quad w \geq 0 \]

The risk_aversion field in MarketData controls \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Equal Risk Contribution (Risk Parity)
docs.text:
Maillard, Roncalli & Teïletche (2010) propose portfolios where every asset contributes the same amount of marginal risk to the portfolio.

The marginal risk contribution of asset \(i\) is:

\[ \text{MRC}_i = \frac{\partial \sigma_p}{\partial w_i} = \frac{(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p} \]

The total risk contribution of asset \(i\) is:

\[ \text{TRC}_i = w_i \cdot \text{MRC}_i = \frac{w_i (\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p} \]

ERC requires \(\text{TRC}_i = \text{TRC}_j\) for all \(i, j\). This is achieved by solving the equivalent convex problem:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln y_i \]

Then normalize: \(w_i = y_i / \sum_j y_j\)

docs.title: Risk Budgeting
docs.text:
Generalizes ERC by assigning target risk budgets \(b_i \geq 0\) (with \(\sum b_i = 1\)) to each asset:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} b_i \ln y_i \]

When \(b_i = 1/N\) for all \(i\), this reduces to Risk Parity. Pass budgets via MarketData.features["risk_budgets"].

docs.title: Maximum Diversification
docs.text:
Choueifaty & Coignard (2008) define the Diversification Ratio:

\[ D(w) = \frac{w^\top \sigma}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \sigma_i}{\sigma_p} \]

where \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\Sigma_{ii}}\) is the individual asset volatility and \(\sigma_p = \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}\) is the portfolio volatility.

The maximum diversification portfolio maximizes \(D(w)\), which is equivalent (via the same substitution trick as Max Sharpe) to:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sigma^\top y = 1 \]

Recover weights: \(w^* = y^* / \mathbf{1}^\top y^*\)

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Allocator Optimization Problem Requires Returns? Equal Weight \(w_i = 1/N\) No Min Volatility \(\min w^\top \Sigma w\) No Max Sharpe \(\min y^\top \Sigma y \text{ s.t. } (\mu-r_f)^\top y=1\) Yes Max Utility \(\max \mu^\top w - \lambda w^\top \Sigma w\) Yes Risk Parity \(\min \frac{1}{2}y^\top\Sigma y - \sum\ln y_i\) No Risk Budgeting \(\min \frac{1}{2}y^\top\Sigma y - \sum b_i\ln y_i\) No Max Diversification \(\min y^\top\Sigma y \text{ s.t. } \sigma^\top y=1\) No

docs.title: References & Papers
docs.text: PyAlloq's algorithms are grounded in seminal academic research. This page provides full citations, summaries, and links to the papers that inspired each component.

docs.title: Markowitz (1952) — Portfolio Selection
docs.text:
Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. The Journal of Finance, 7(1), 77–91. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x

Contribution: Foundational mean-variance framework. Introduced the concept of the efficient frontier — the set of portfolios offering maximum expected return for a given level of risk.

Key formula: [ \min_w w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mu^\top w = \mu^*, \; \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1 ]

Implemented in: MarkowitzAllocator (MIN_VOLATILITY, MAX_SHARPE, MAX_RETURN)

docs.title: Maillard, Roncalli & Teïletche (2010) — Equal Risk Contributions
docs.text:
Maillard, S., Roncalli, T., & Teïletche, J. (2010). The Properties of Equally Weighted Risk Contributions Portfolios. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 36(4), 60–70. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2010.36.4.060

Contribution: Defined the Equal Risk Contribution (ERC) portfolio — a practical middle ground between Equal Weight and Minimum Variance. Showed that ERC portfolios can be computed via a convex optimization problem.

Key formula: [ w_i (\Sigma w)_i = w_j (\Sigma w)_j \quad \forall i, j ]

Implemented in: RiskParityAllocator, RiskBudgetingAllocator

docs.title: Choueifaty & Coignard (2008) — Maximum Diversification
docs.text:
Choueifaty, Y., & Coignard, Y. (2008). Toward Maximum Diversification. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 35(1), 40–51. https://doi.org/10.3905/JPM.2008.35.1.40

Contribution: Introduced the Diversification Ratio as a measure of portfolio diversification. The Maximum Diversification portfolio maximizes this ratio.

Key formula: [ D(w) = \frac{w^\top \sigma}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} ]

Implemented in: MaxDiversificationAllocator

docs.title: López de Prado (2016) — Hierarchical Risk Parity
docs.text:
López de Prado, M. (2016). Building Diversified Portfolios that Outperform Out-of-Sample. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 42(4), 59–69. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2016.42.4.059 arXiv:1603.05831

Contribution: Proposed HRP — a machine learning approach to portfolio construction that avoids covariance matrix inversion. Uses hierarchical clustering and recursive bisection to allocate weights in a tree-like structure.

Steps: Distance matrix → Hierarchical clustering → Quasi-diagonalization → Recursive bisection

Implemented in: HRPAllocator

docs.title: Black & Litterman (1992) — Global Portfolio Optimization
docs.text:
Black, F., & Litterman, R. (1992). Global Portfolio Optimization. Financial Analysts Journal, 48(5), 28–43. https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v48.n5.28

Contribution: Combined CAPM equilibrium returns with subjective investor views through Bayesian updating. Produces more stable and intuitive return estimates than pure historical means.

Key formula: [ \mu^* = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} \Pi + P^\top \Omega^{-1} Q\right] ]

Implemented in: BlackLittermanEstimator

docs.title: Ledoit & Wolf (2004) — Shrinkage Estimation
docs.text:
Ledoit, O., & Wolf, M. (2004). Honey, I Shrunk the Sample Covariance Matrix. The Journal of Portfolio Management, 30(4), 110–119. https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2004.110

Contribution: Derived an analytically optimal shrinkage intensity for the sample covariance matrix, providing a closed-form, well-conditioned estimator that improves out-of-sample performance for Markowitz optimization.

Key formula: [ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^ \hat{\mu}_{cov} I ]

Implemented in: LedoitWolfEstimator

docs.title: Almgren & Chriss (2001) — Optimal Execution
docs.text:
Almgren, R., & Chriss, N. (2001). Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions. Journal of Risk, 3, 5–39. https://doi.org/10.21314/JOR.2001.041

Contribution: Derived an optimal trade execution strategy that minimizes total transaction costs (market impact + risk) for a given liquidation horizon. The market impact cost model is widely used in institutional portfolio management.

Market impact formula: [ \text{impact}_i = \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\text{trade_size}_i}{\text{daily_volume}_i}} ]

Implemented in: AlmgrenChrissCostModel

docs.title: Meucci (2008) — Fully Flexible Views: Theory and Practice
docs.text:
Meucci, A. (2008). Fully Flexible Views: Theory and Practice. Risk, 21(10), 97–102. https://ssrn.com/abstract=1213325

Contribution: Introduced Entropy Pooling to blend arbitrary non-Gaussian Monte Carlo distributions with linear equality and inequality views on returns, volatilities, and correlations via Relative Entropy (Kullback-Leibler) minimization solved in the low-dimensional Lagrange dual space.

Key formula: [ x^* = \arg\min_{x \in \Delta^M} \sum_{m=1}^M x_m \ln!\left(\frac{x_m}{p_m}\right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad A x \le b, \; C x = d ]

Implemented in: EntropyPooler, ViewBuilder (AbsoluteView, RelativeView, VolatilityView, CovarianceView)

docs.title: Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos & Vosper (1999) — Filtered Historical Simulation
docs.text:
Barone-Adesi, G., Giannopoulos, K., & Vosper, L. (1999). VaR Without Correlations for Portfolios of Derivative Securities. Journal of Futures Markets, 19(5), 583–602.

Contribution: Combined parametric GARCH volatility filtration with non-parametric historical residual bootstrapping, preserving empirical fat tails and cross-asset co-movement while adapting dynamically to current volatility regimes.

Implemented in: FHSGenerator

docs.title: McNeil & Frey (2000) & Demarta & McNeil (2005) — GARCH-EVT & Student-\(t\) Copula
docs.text:
McNeil, A. J., & Frey, R. (2000). Estimation of Tail-Related Risk Measures for Heteroscedastic Financial Time Series: An Extreme Value Approach. Journal of Empirical Finance, 7(3–4), 271–300.

Demarta, S., & McNeil, A. J. (2005). The \(t\) Copula and Related Copulas. International Statistical Review, 73(1), 111–129.

Contribution: Modeled conditional heteroscedasticity via AR-GARCH filtration, fitted Generalized Pareto Distributions (GPD) to extreme tail exceedances, and coupled marginals with a Student-\(t\) Copula to capture asymmetric tail risk and positive lower-tail crash dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)).

Implemented in: GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator

docs.title: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2017) — Probability of Backtest Overfitting
docs.text:
Bailey, D. H., Borwein, J., López de Prado, M., & Zhu, Q. J. (2017). The Probability of Backtest Overfitting. Journal of Computational Finance, 20(4), 39–69. https://ssrn.com/abstract=2326253

Contribution: Introduced the non-parametric Combinatorial Symmetric Cross-Validation (CSCV) framework to estimate the probability that a strategy configuration selected for optimal In-Sample performance underperforms the median Out-of-Sample (\(\text{PBO} = \mathbb{P}[\lambda_c \le 0]\)).

Implemented in: PBOEvaluator, plot_pbo_distribution, RobustnessTearSheet

docs.title: López de Prado (2018) — Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation
docs.text:
López de Prado, M. (2018). Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley. (Chapter 12: Backtesting through Cross-Validation).

Contribution: Formulated Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) to eliminate look-ahead leakage via purging and embargoing while generating \(\varphi(N, k) = \binom{N-1}{k-1}\) complete out-of-sample backtest paths across recombined market regimes.

Implemented in: CPCVSplitter, plot_cpcv_paths, RobustnessTearSheet

docs.title: Allocators
docs.text: Allocators solve for optimal portfolio weights given market data, a covariance matrix, and optionally expected returns. All allocators implement BaseAllocator and can be dropped into any StrategyPipeline.

docs.title: Equal Weight (EqualWeightAllocator)
docs.text:
Assigns identical weight \(1/N\) to every asset. The simplest possible portfolio. Surprisingly hard to beat out-of-sample.

\[ w_i = \frac{1}{N}, \quad \forall i \] 
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.naive import EqualWeightAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

Use as a baseline

Always include EqualWeightAllocator as a benchmark in your backtest comparisons.

docs.title: Markowitz (MarkowitzAllocator)
docs.text:
Classical mean-variance optimizer. Supports three objective functions via the ObjectiveFunction enum.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction
Min VolatilityMax SharpeMax Return (Utility)

Minimizes total portfolio variance with no expected return input needed.

\[ \min_w \; w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1,\; w \geq 0 \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY
)

Maximizes the Sharpe ratio using the Tobin substitution trick. Requires expected returns.

\[ \max_w \frac{w^\top \mu - r_f}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \;\equiv\; \min_y \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (\mu - r_f)^\top y = 1,\; y \geq 0 \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE
)
# MAX_SHARPE requires a returns estimator in the pipeline
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
)

Maximizes mean-variance utility, controlled by risk_aversion in MarketData.

\[ \max_w \; \mu^\top w - \lambda \cdot w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1,\; w \geq 0 \] 
allocator = MarkowitzAllocator(
    tickers=data.assets,
    objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_RETURN
)

docs.title: Risk Parity (RiskParityAllocator)
docs.text:
Equal Risk Contribution (ERC). Every asset contributes the same amount of marginal risk to the portfolio. No expected return input needed — purely covariance-driven.

\[ \min_y \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln y_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y \geq 0 \]

Then normalize: \(w = y / \mathbf{1}^\top y\)

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Risk Budgeting (RiskBudgetingAllocator)
docs.text:
Generalization of Risk Parity where each asset is assigned a target risk budget \(b_i\). If no budgets are provided, defaults to equal budgeting (identical to Risk Parity).

\[ \min_y \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} b_i \ln y_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y \geq 0 \] 
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_budgeting import RiskBudgetingAllocator
import pandas as pd

# Provide risk budgets through MarketData.features
risk_budgets = pd.DataFrame(
    {"AAPL": [0.4], "MSFT": [0.3], "GOOGL": [0.3]},
    index=data.prices.index[:1]
).reindex(data.prices.index).ffill()

data_with_budgets = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features={"risk_budgets": risk_budgets},
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskBudgetingAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Max Diversification (MaxDiversificationAllocator)
docs.text:
Maximizes the Diversification Ratio — the weighted sum of individual asset volatilities divided by portfolio volatility.

\[ \max_w \; D(w) = \frac{w^\top \sigma}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \]

Implemented via the equivalent dual: minimize portfolio variance subject to weighted volatilities summing to 1.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.max_diversification import MaxDiversificationAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MaxDiversificationAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Graph-Based ML Allocators
docs.text: These allocators use hierarchical clustering on the correlation matrix to build a dendrogram-based weight allocation. They do not invert the covariance matrix, making them more numerically stable for large universes.

docs.title: HRP (HRPAllocator)
docs.text:
Hierarchical Risk Parity (López de Prado, 2016). Uses single-linkage clustering on correlation distance, quasi-diagonalization of the covariance matrix, and recursive bisection to assign inverse-variance weights.

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

Steps: 1. Compute correlation distance matrix: \(d_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho_{ij}}{2}}\) 2. Build hierarchical cluster tree (dendrogram) 3. Sort assets by quasi-diagonalization 4. Assign weights via recursive bisection using cluster inverse-variance portfolios

docs.title: HERC (HERCAllocator)
docs.text:
Hierarchical Equal Risk Contribution. Similar to HRP but allocates risk budget equally across the hierarchical clusters at each level, then inverse-variance within each cluster.

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.herc import HERCAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=HERCAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: NCO (NCOAllocator)
docs.text:
Nested Cluster Optimization. Divides the universe into clusters via k-means on the correlation matrix, runs a Markowitz optimization within each cluster (intra-cluster), and then a second Markowitz optimization across cluster representatives (inter-cluster).

from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.nco import NCOAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=NCOAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

docs.title: Choosing an Allocator
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Allocator Quick baseline EqualWeightAllocator Minimize portfolio risk, no return forecast needed RiskParityAllocator Minimize portfolio risk, trust your return forecast MarkowitzAllocator(MIN_VOLATILITY) Maximize Sharpe, have a good return model MarkowitzAllocator(MAX_SHARPE) Large universe (50+ assets), covariance unstable HRPAllocator or NCOAllocator Maximize portfolio diversification MaxDiversificationAllocator Assign specific risk budgets per asset RiskBudgetingAllocator

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Allocator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseAllocator
from pyalloq_core.results import OptimizationResult
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyCustomAllocator(BaseAllocator):
    def allocate(
        self,
        data: MarketData,
        cov_matrix: pd.DataFrame,
        expected_returns: pd.Series | None = None,
        **kwargs,
    ) -> OptimizationResult:
        # Your optimization logic here
        weights = pd.Series(1.0 / len(data.assets), index=data.assets)
        return OptimizationResult(weights=weights, status="OPTIMAL")

# Drop it into any pipeline — no other changes needed
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=MyCustomAllocator(tickers=data.assets))

docs.title: Backtesting
docs.text: WalkForwardEngine runs your StrategyPipeline across historical data, rebalancing at regular intervals, and accounts for transaction costs — with a zero-lookahead guarantee at every step.

docs.title: WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",                        # monthly rebalancing
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(252),         # 1-year rolling lookback
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0),       # 10 bps per trade
)

results = engine.run(data)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description pipeline StrategyPipeline required The strategy to backtest rebalance_freq str "ME" Pandas offset alias: "ME" (monthly), "W" (weekly), "QE" (quarterly) splitter BaseWindowSplitter RollingWindowSplitter(252) Controls how historical windows are sliced cost_model BaseCostModel FlatBpsCostModel(10.0) Transaction cost model applied at each rebalance

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
results = engine.run(data)

results["returns"]     # pd.Series — daily portfolio returns (net of costs)
results["weights"]     # pd.DataFrame — daily forward-filled weights
results["tear_sheet"]  # pd.DataFrame — performance summary

docs.title: Window Splitters
docs.text: The splitter controls how much historical data is visible to the pipeline at each rebalance date.

docs.title: Rolling Window (RollingWindowSplitter)
docs.text:
Uses a fixed-length lookback window. The window slides forward with each rebalance. Only rebalance dates with enough history (≥ lookback_window observations) are included.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter

# Use exactly 1 year (252 trading days) of history at each rebalance
splitter = RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=252)

When to use: You want a consistent amount of data at each period, ignoring older observations. Appropriate for estimators sensitive to regime change.

docs.title: Expanding Window (ExpandingWindowSplitter)
docs.text:
Uses all available history up to each rebalance date, with a minimum threshold to start.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter

# Start backtesting once 252 days of data are available; use all history thereafter
splitter = ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252)

When to use: When longer history improves estimator stability (e.g., Ledoit-Wolf, sample covariance), and you don't expect structural breaks.

docs.title: Purged K-Fold (PurgedKFoldSplitter)
docs.text:
Used for ML model training and cross-validation, not for backtesting. Splits data into K folds and applies an embargo (gap between train and test sets) to prevent information leakage from overlapping return windows.

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import PurgedKFoldSplitter

splitter = PurgedKFoldSplitter(n_splits=5, embargo_pct=0.01)

for train_data, test_data in splitter.split(data):
    model.fit(train_data)
    predictions = model.predict(test_data)

Not for standard backtesting

PurgedKFoldSplitter is designed for ML training loops, not for WalkForwardEngine. Use RollingWindowSplitter or ExpandingWindowSplitter for standard portfolio backtests.

docs.title: Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation & Scrambling (CPCVSplitter & PBOEvaluator)
docs.text:
To guard against backtest overfitting and chronological regime luck, pyalloq-backtest includes Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCVSplitter) and Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBOEvaluator):

  1. Regime Scrambling (CPCVSplitter.scramble_timelines): Partitions historical strategy returns into \(N\) chronological regime blocks and recombines them into scrambled timelines to test whether a strategy's Sharpe ratio and drawdowns survive when the sequence of market regimes is reordered.
  2. Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBOEvaluator):
  3. evaluate_cscv(strategy_returns_matrix): Runs Bailey & López de Prado's Combinatorial Symmetric Cross-Validation (CSCV) across a \((T \times M)\) matrix of \(M\) strategy trials to compute the exact probability that the In-Sample optimal strategy underperforms the median Out-of-Sample (\(\mathbb{P}[\lambda_c \le 0]\)).
  4. evaluate_benchmark(historical_result, cpcv_or_mc_result): Evaluates a single strategy's historical Sharpe against a distribution of CPCV or Monte Carlo paths.
from pyalloq_backtest import CPCVSplitter, PBOEvaluator

# 1. Scramble historical backtest across 6 regime blocks
cpcv = CPCVSplitter(n_groups=6, k_test_groups=2, max_paths=100)
cpcv_result = cpcv.scramble_timelines(results)

# 2. Evaluate single-strategy survival vs. scrambled timelines
pbo_eval = PBOEvaluator(n_partitions=8)
pbo_bench = pbo_eval.evaluate_benchmark(results, cpcv_result)
print(f"Prob(OOS Sharpe < 0): {pbo_bench.prob_oos_loss:.1%}")

Interactive Robustness Visualizations

Pass results, cpcv_result, or pbo_result directly to RobustnessTearSheet in pyalloq-viz to plot Rank Logit distributions, IS-vs-OOS Sharpe degradation, and scrambled equity cones.

docs.title: Flat Bps (FlatBpsCostModel)
docs.text:
A flat percentage fee applied to the absolute change in weights at each rebalance. Suitable for retail or small-AUM use cases.

\[ \text{cost}_i = |\Delta w_i| \times \frac{\text{bps}}{10000} \] 
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import FlatBpsCostModel

cost_model = FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0)  # 10 basis points per unit of turnover

docs.title: Almgren-Chriss (AlmgrenChrissCostModel)
docs.text:
Non-linear market impact cost model. Models both fixed bid-ask spread and non-linear price impact proportional to trade size relative to daily volume.

\[ \text{cost}_i = \left(\text{spread} + \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\text{trade\_size}_i}{\text{volume}_i}}\right) \times |\Delta w_i| \] 
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

cost_model = AlmgrenChrissCostModel(
    portfolio_aum=1_000_000,  # portfolio size in USD
    spread_bps=2.0,            # bid-ask spread
    gamma=0.1,                 # market impact coefficient
)

Requires volume data

AlmgrenChrissCostModel requires data.features["volume"] to be set on your MarketData. Volume is used to compute trade size as a fraction of daily market volume.

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={"volume": volume_df},
)

docs.title: Performance Metrics (TearSheet)
docs.text:
MetricsTearSheet.generate(portfolio_returns) produces a summary table of key performance metrics.

Metric Formula Description total_return \((1+r)^{T} - 1\) Cumulative return over full period annualized_return \((1 + \text{total\_return})^{1/Y} - 1\) Geometric annualized return annualized_volatility \(\sigma_r \times \sqrt{252}\) Annualized standard deviation sharpe_ratio \(\frac{r_a - r_f}{\sigma_a}\) Risk-adjusted return maximum_drawdown \(\min_t \frac{V_t - \max_{\tau \leq t} V_\tau}{\max_{\tau \leq t} V_\tau}\) Largest peak-to-trough decline calmar_ratio (\frac{r_a}{ \text{MDD} 
from pyalloq_backtest.metrics import MetricsTearSheet

tear_sheet = MetricsTearSheet.generate(
    portfolio_returns=results["returns"],
    risk_free_rate=0.04,
)
print(tear_sheet)

docs.title: Full Backtest Example
docs.text:
from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN"],
    start="2018-01-01", end="2024-01-01",
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",
    splitter=ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252),
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=5.0),
)

results = engine.run(data)
print(results["tear_sheet"])

docs.title: Covariance Estimators
docs.text:
Covariance estimators produce an NxN annualized covariance matrix from a MarketData object. The choice of estimator has a major impact on optimizer stability, especially for Markowitz-family allocators.

All estimators implement BaseCovarianceEstimator:

class BaseCovarianceEstimator(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.DataFrame:
        ...

docs.title: Empirical (EmpiricalCovariance)
docs.text:
The classical sample covariance matrix. Simple and unbiased, but sensitive to outliers and unreliable when the number of observations \(T\) is close to the number of assets \(N\).

\[ \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T} (r_t - \bar{r})(r_t - \bar{r})^\top \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.empirical import EmpiricalCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=EmpiricalCovariance(),
)

When to use: Large \(T/N\) ratio (e.g., 10+ years of daily data for 20 stocks). Stable, liquid markets.

docs.title: EWMA (EWMACovariance)
docs.text:
Exponentially Weighted Moving Average covariance. More recent observations receive exponentially higher weight, capturing volatility clustering (GARCH-like behaviour).

\[ \hat{\Sigma}_t = (1-\lambda) r_{t} r_{t}^\top + \lambda \hat{\Sigma}_{t-1} \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ewma import EWMACovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=EWMACovariance(span=120),  # 120-day span
)

When to use: Volatile or crisis periods where recent correlations matter more. Time-varying risk models.

docs.title: Ledoit-Wolf (LedoitWolfShrinkage)
docs.text:
Analytically optimal shrinkage of the sample covariance towards a structured target (e.g., identity or scaled identity). Minimizes mean squared error of the estimator.

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^*) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^* \mu \mathbf{I} \]

where \(\alpha^*\) is the analytically derived optimal shrinkage intensity.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

When to use: High-dimensional portfolios (\(N > 50\)), short histories. The go-to robust estimator for Markowitz optimization.

See: Ledoit & Wolf (2004)

docs.title: Random Matrix Theory (RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator)
docs.text:
Filters the empirical covariance matrix by removing noise eigenvalues that fall below the Marchenko-Pastur upper bound. These eigenvalues are statistical artifacts of finite sample size, not true economic factors.

Denoising step: Any eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) below the Marchenko-Pastur bound \(\lambda_+\) is replaced by the average noise eigenvalue:

\[ \lambda_+ = \sigma^2 \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{T}}\right)^2 \]

Detoning step (optional): Removes the largest eigenvalue (the "market mode") to isolate sector-level correlations.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.random_matrix_theory import RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator(
        denoise=True,   # remove noise eigenvalues
        detone=False,   # keep the market factor
    ),
)

When to use: Large universes where the empirical correlation matrix is dominated by noise. Pairs well with HRP and NCO allocators.

See: López de Prado (2020) — Advances in Financial Machine Learning

docs.title: Semi-Covariance (SemiCovariance)
docs.text:
Computes covariance using only downside returns (negative returns). This targets downside risk specifically, which is more relevant for loss-averse investors than full variance.

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{semi}_{ij} = \frac{1}{T^-} \sum_{t: r_{i,t} < 0} r_{i,t} \cdot r_{j,t} \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.semi_covariance import SemiCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=SemiCovariance(),
)

When to use: When minimizing downside risk is the primary objective. Pairs naturally with MarkowitzAllocator(MIN_VOLATILITY) for drawdown-conscious portfolios.

docs.title: Choosing a Covariance Estimator
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Estimator Many observations, stable market EmpiricalCovariance Volatile regime, recent correlations important EWMACovariance High-dimensional, short history LedoitWolfShrinkage Large universe, correlation noise removal RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator Downside risk focus SemiCovariance

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Covariance Estimator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseCovarianceEstimator
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyCovariance(BaseCovarianceEstimator):
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.DataFrame:
        returns = data.prices.pct_change().dropna()
        return returns.cov() * 252

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    cov_estimator=MyCovariance(),
)

docs.title: Data Connectors
docs.text: Data connectors fetch raw market data from external vendors and normalize it into a standardized MarketData object. All connectors inherit from BaseDataConnector.

docs.title: Yahoo Finance (YahooFinanceClient)
docs.text:
Free, no API key required. Suitable for research and prototyping.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient

client = YahooFinanceClient()
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN"],
    start="2020-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

docs.title: Alpha Vantage (AlphaVantageClient)
docs.text:
Requires a free or premium API key from alphavantage.co.

from pyalloq_data_connector.alpha_vantage import AlphaVantageClient

client = AlphaVantageClient(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT"],
    start="2022-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

docs.title: Finnhub (FinnhubClient)
docs.text:
Real-time and historical stock data. Requires an API key from finnhub.io.

from pyalloq_data_connector.finnhub import FinnhubClient

client = FinnhubClient(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT"],
    start="2023-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

docs.title: EOD Historical Data (EODClient)
docs.text:
Comprehensive global market data. Requires an API key from eodhd.com.

from pyalloq_data_connector.eod import EODClient

client = EODClient(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL.US", "MSFT.US"],
    start="2020-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

docs.title: Adding Features to MarketData
docs.text:
After fetching prices, attach time-series features to your MarketData:

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

# Fetch volume separately if your connector doesn't include it
volume_df = ...  # pd.DataFrame with same index as data.prices

enriched_data = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features={
        "volume": volume_df,
    },
    risk_free_rate=0.04,
)

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Connector
docs.text:
from pyalloq_data_connector.base import BaseDataConnector
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyDataConnector(BaseDataConnector):
    def get_market_data(
        self, tickers: list[str], start: str, end: str
    ) -> MarketData:
        # fetch from your data source
        prices = pd.DataFrame(...)
        return MarketData(prices=prices)

docs.title: Feature Engineering
docs.text: pyalloq-features provides tools to compute and attach time-series features — technical indicators, cross-sectional signals, and scaled inputs — to your MarketData. Features flow through the entire pipeline, enabling advanced estimators and ML models.

docs.title: Technical Transformers
docs.text:
Compute price-based technical indicators from MarketData.prices.

from pyalloq_features.transformers.technical import TechnicalTransformer

transformer = TechnicalTransformer()
features = transformer.transform(data)

# features is a dict[str, pd.DataFrame] ready to attach to MarketData

Available indicators include momentum, rolling volatility, RSI, and moving average crossovers. Each indicator is computed per-asset and aligned to the price index to prevent look-ahead bias.

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

enriched = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices,
    features=features,
)

docs.title: Cross-Sectional Transformers
docs.text:
Compute cross-sectional signals — ranking assets relative to each other at each point in time.

from pyalloq_features.transformers.cross_sectional import CrossSectionalTransformer

cs_transformer = CrossSectionalTransformer()
cs_features = cs_transformer.transform(data)

Cross-sectional features are particularly useful with FactorReturnEstimator and custom ML-based allocators.

docs.title: Scalers
docs.text:
Normalize features before feeding them to ML estimators or deep learning models.

from pyalloq_features.scalers import StandardFeatureScaler

scaler = StandardFeatureScaler()
scaled_features = scaler.fit_transform(features)

docs.title: Attaching Features to MarketData
docs.text:
Features must share the exact same DatetimeIndex as data.prices — MarketData.validate_alignment() enforces this at construction.

from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={
        "momentum":   momentum_df,    # time-series momentum signals
        "volume":     volume_df,      # daily volume (required by AlmgrenChriss)
        "risk_budgets": budgets_df,   # target risk allocations (for RiskBudgetingAllocator)
    },
)

docs.title: Using Features in Estimators
docs.text:
Several components read from MarketData.features:

Feature key Used by "risk_budgets" RiskBudgetingAllocator "volume" AlmgrenChrissCostModel Any factor data FactorReturnEstimator Any signal Custom ML estimators / DL models

docs.title: Monte Carlo Simulation & Entropy Pooling
docs.text: pyalloq-simulation provides a complete synthetic scenario engine for stress-testing portfolio strategies, expressing non-Gaussian market views via Meucci's Entropy Pooling, and running parallel multi-path walk-forward backtests across thousands of synthetic market realities.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    MD["📦 MarketData\nHistorical Prices & Features"]
    IMP["🩹 FactorBackcastImputer\nPre-IPO & Gap Imputation"]
    GEN["🎲 ScenarioGenerator\nGaussian / PCA / FHS / Copula / GMM"]
    SMD["🧊 ScenarioMarketData\n3D Tensor (M, T, N)"]
    VB["🔭 ViewBuilder & EntropyPooler\n1st & 2nd Moment Views"]
    EV["📉 ScenarioEvaluator\nCVaR, View-Adjusted MDD, Ruin"]
    PME["⚡ ParallelMonteCarloEngine\nMulti-Path WalkForwardEngine"]

    MD --> IMP --> GEN --> SMD
    SMD --> VB --> EV
    SMD --> PME

docs.title: 1. Missing Data Imputation (FactorBackcastImputer)
docs.text:
When your portfolio universe includes recent IPOs or assets with interior data gaps, a naive .dropna() truncates the entire \(N\)-asset matrix down to the shortest asset's history.

FactorBackcastImputer preserves the full historical length \(T\) by extracting principal component factors from anchor assets in return space, regressing partial-history assets onto those factors, injecting matched idiosyncratic volatility, and back-casting continuous price paths.

from pyalloq_simulation import FactorBackcastImputer

imputer = FactorBackcastImputer(
    n_components=3,
    min_coverage=0.85,
    inject_idiosyncratic_noise=True,
)
clean_data = imputer.fit_transform(raw_market_data)

Automatic Imputation in Generators

Every scenario generator enables impute_missing=True by default, automatically applying FactorBackcastImputer inside .fit(data) whenever missing observations are detected.

docs.title: 2. Scenario Generators
docs.text:
All generators implement BaseScenarioGenerator and output a ScenarioMarketData 3D tensor of shape (M, T, N) (n_paths × horizon × n_assets), along with forward-projected pd.DatetimeIndex timestamps and jointly synthesized exogenous features.
