Generator Distribution & Dynamics Best Used For GaussianGenerator Multivariate Normal with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage & Cholesky factorization Fast baseline testing and isolating optimizer behavior PCAFactorGenerator \(K\) latent PCA factors + idiosyncratic Gaussian noise High-dimensional portfolios (\(N \gg K\)) FHSGenerator Univariate GARCH(1,1) filtering + synchronous empirical residual bootstrap Preserving historical volatility clustering and empirical fat tails GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) marginals + Generalized Pareto (EVT) tails + Student-\(t\) Copula Modeling extreme tail risk and simultaneous crash dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)) GMMRegimeGenerator \(K\)-state Gaussian Mixture Model + Markov transition matrix Stress-testing structural breaks and Bull/Bear regime shifts

docs.title: Generating Scenarios
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pyalloq_simulation import (
    GaussianGenerator,
    PCAFactorGenerator,
    FHSGenerator,
    GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator,
    GMMRegimeGenerator,
)

# Example: GARCH-EVT-Student-t Copula Generator
generator = GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator(
    nu=5.0,
    lower_quantile=0.10,
    upper_quantile=0.90,
    dtype=np.float32,
    impute_missing=True,
)
generator.fit(data, log_returns=False)

scenario_data = generator.generate(n_paths=2000, horizon=252)
print(scenario_data.prices.shape)  # (2000, 252, N)

docs.title: Memory Management & Tensor Batching
docs.text:
A \(10,000 \times 252 \times 500\) simulation in float64 consumes over 20 GB of RAM across price and return tensors. To prevent out-of-memory (OOM) spikes in cloud containers or parallel workers:

  1. Precision Control: All generators default to dtype=np.float32 (configurable to np.float64).
  2. Streamed Batch Generation: Use generate_batches() to yield memory-bounded ScenarioMarketData chunks:
for batch in generator.generate_batches(n_paths=10_000, horizon=252, batch_size=1_000):
    # Each batch holds only (1000, 252, N) in float32
    process_batch(batch)

docs.title: 3. Expressing Market Views & Entropy Pooling
docs.text: Unlike Black-Litterman—which is restricted to normal distributions and linear return views—Meucci's Entropy Pooling blends any non-Gaussian Monte Carlo prior with first-moment (return) and second-moment (volatility and correlation/covariance) views by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between prior probabilities \(p\) and posterior probabilities \(x^*\).

docs.title: Supported View Types
docs.text:
View Class Moment Example AbsoluteView 1st (Return) "AAPL cumulative return >= 5%" RelativeView 1st (Spread) "MSFT outperforms GOOGL by >= 2%" VolatilityView 2nd (Volatility) "AAPL volatility increases by 50% (multiplier=1.5)" CovarianceView 2nd (Correlation / Covariance) "AAPL–MSFT correlation >= 0.60" 
from pyalloq_simulation import (
    AbsoluteView,
    RelativeView,
    VolatilityView,
    CovarianceView,
    ViewBuilder,
    EntropyPooler,
)

views = [
    AbsoluteView(asset="AAPL", operator="==", target=0.08),
    RelativeView(asset_outperformer="MSFT", asset_underperformer="AMZN", operator=">=", target=0.02),
    VolatilityView(asset="AAPL", operator=">=", multiplier=1.50),
    CovarianceView(asset_1="AAPL", asset_2="MSFT", operator=">=", target_correlation=0.50),
]

builder = ViewBuilder(scenario_data)
A_ineq, b_ineq, C_eq, d_eq = builder.build(views)

pooler = EntropyPooler(n_scenarios=scenario_data.n_paths)
entropy_result = pooler.fit(A_ineq=A_ineq, b_ineq=b_ineq, C_eq=C_eq, d_eq=d_eq)

print(f"Converged: {entropy_result.success}, KL Divergence: {entropy_result.kl_divergence:.4f}")

docs.title: 4. Path-Dependent Risk Evaluation (ScenarioEvaluator)
docs.text:
Terminal metrics alone miss intra-horizon crashes that trigger margin calls or risk limits. ScenarioEvaluator evaluates both terminal and intra-horizon path metrics across all \(t \in [0, T]\) weighted by the posterior scenario probabilities entropy_result.weights:

  • expected_return: Posterior probability-weighted cumulative return.
  • volatility: Posterior probability-weighted return standard deviation.
  • sharpe_ratio: View-adjusted horizon Sharpe ratio.
  • cvar_95: Posterior probability-weighted 95% Conditional Value-at-Risk (Expected Shortfall).
  • view_adjusted_mdd: Posterior probability-weighted Maximum Drawdown across the \((M, T+1)\) wealth trajectory.
  • probability_of_ruin: Posterior probability mass of paths whose intra-horizon drawdown or equity drop breaches ruin_threshold (default -0.30, i.e., a 30% loss).
import numpy as np
from pyalloq_simulation import ScenarioEvaluator

evaluator = ScenarioEvaluator(risk_free_rate=0.03, ruin_threshold=-0.30)
weights = np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25])

metrics = evaluator.evaluate(
    scenario_data=scenario_data,
    asset_weights=weights,
    entropy_result=entropy_result,
)

print(f"Expected Return:     {metrics.expected_return:.2%}")
print(f"CVaR (95%):          {metrics.cvar_95:.2%}")
print(f"View-Adjusted MDD:   {metrics.view_adjusted_mdd:.2%}")
print(f"Probability of Ruin: {metrics.probability_of_ruin:.2%}")

docs.title: 5. Multi-Path Strategy Backtesting (ParallelMonteCarloEngine)
docs.text: To evaluate how a full StrategyPipeline and WalkForwardEngine perform across hundreds or thousands of synthetic market paths, use ParallelMonteCarloEngine (also aliased as MonteCarloEngine in pyalloq_core.engines).

docs.title: Hybrid Feature Synthesis for Deep Learning & Technical Indicators
docs.text:
1. Exogenous Features (data.features): Automatically projected inside every BaseScenarioGenerator conditioned on simulated asset returns so Deep Learning estimators (such as DeepCovarianceEstimator) receive aligned 3D feature tensors.
  2. Endogenous Technical Features (FeaturePipeline): Pass a FeaturePipeline to ParallelMonteCarloEngine(feature_pipeline=...) to deterministically recompute price-derived indicators (e.g., RSI, MACD, rolling volatility) on each synthetic path inside the worker pool.
from pyalloq_core.engines import ParallelMonteCarloEngine
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq_features.core.pipeline import FeaturePipeline
from pyalloq_simulation import GaussianGenerator

# 1. Fit generator on historical MarketData
gen = GaussianGenerator()
gen.fit(data)

# 2. Configure standard WalkForwardEngine
pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets))
wf_engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=60),
    rebalance_freq="ME",
)

# 3. Execute across streamed scenario batches in parallel
mc_engine = ParallelMonteCarloEngine(
    backtest_engine=wf_engine,
    max_workers=4,
    feature_pipeline=FeaturePipeline(),  # optional per-path feature transformers
)

batches = gen.generate_batches(n_paths=100, horizon=252, batch_size=25)
mc_result = mc_engine.run_batches(batches)

print(mc_result.equity_curves.shape)          # (T, 100)
print(mc_result.metrics_distribution.head())  # Distribution of Sharpe, MDD, Sortino across paths

docs.title: Return Estimators
docs.text:
Return estimators produce a pd.Series of annualized expected returns — one per asset — given a MarketData object. The result is consumed by StrategyPipeline and passed to the allocator.

All estimators implement BaseReturnEstimator:

class BaseReturnEstimator(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.Series:
        ...

docs.title: EWMA (EWMAReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Exponentially Weighted Moving Average returns. Recent observations receive higher weight. The default estimator in StrategyPipeline.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.ewma import EWMAReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=EWMAReturnEstimator(span=60),  # 60-day span
)

When to use: When you believe recent performance is more predictive than long-run historical averages.

docs.title: James-Stein (JamesSteinReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Shrinks historical mean returns towards the grand cross-sectional mean. Reduces estimation error in high-dimensional settings. Optimal for universes with \(N \geq 3\) assets.

\[ \hat{\mu}^{JS} = (1 - w) \hat{\mu} + w \bar{\mu} \mathbf{1} \]

where the shrinkage intensity \(w\) is:

\[ w = \min\left(1, \frac{N-2}{(\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})}\right) \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: Large universes (10+ assets) where sample mean is noisy and you want a theoretically grounded shrinkage.

docs.title: Volatility-Scaled Multi-Horizon Momentum (VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator)
docs.text:
Computes raw momentum over multiple lookback horizons (by default 63, 126, and 252 trading days, skipping the most recent 21 days to avoid 1-month short-term reversal). Each horizon return is normalized by realized volatility, and the resulting scores are standardized cross-sectionally to produce stable relative return forecasts.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator(
        horizons=(63, 126, 252),
        skip_period=21,
    ),
)

When to use: Equity or multi-asset universes where momentum signals across varying horizons need to be aggregated and risk-adjusted without letting high-volatility assets dominate.

docs.title: Residual Momentum (ResidualMomentumEstimator)
docs.text:
Isolates idiosyncratic price momentum by regressing each asset's historical returns on a cross-sectional market proxy to remove systemic market beta:

\[ R_{i, t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i R_{m, t} + \epsilon_{i, t} \]

Standardized cumulative residuals \(\sum \epsilon_{i, t} / \sigma_{\epsilon, i}\) are then converted to cross-sectional Z-scores.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import ResidualMomentumEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=ResidualMomentumEstimator(
        lookback=252,
        skip_period=21,
    ),
)

When to use: You want trend-following exposure driven purely by asset-specific performance rather than co-movement with broader equity indices.

docs.title: Factor Returns (MultiFactorReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Estimates expected returns using a factor model. Asset returns are attributed to systematic risk factors (e.g., Fama-French). The factor loadings are estimated from data.features.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.factor import MultiFactorReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=MultiFactorReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: You have factor data attached to MarketData.features and want a structured return model.

docs.title: Implied Returns (ImpliedReturnEstimator)
docs.text:
Reverse-engineers expected returns from observed market-capitalization weights using the Black-Litterman equilibrium formula:

\[ \Pi = \lambda \Sigma w^{mkt} \]

where \(\lambda\) is the implied risk aversion from the market, \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix, and \(w^{mkt}\) are cap-weighted market weights.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.implied import ImpliedReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=ImpliedReturnEstimator(),
)

When to use: You want returns that are consistent with market equilibrium, as a neutral starting point before overlaying views.

docs.title: Black-Litterman (BlackLittermanEstimator)
docs.text:
Blends the market equilibrium returns \(\Pi\) with investor views \(Q\) expressed through a picking matrix \(P\). Returns both a posterior expected return vector and a posterior covariance matrix.

\[ \mu^* = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} \Pi + P^\top \Omega^{-1} Q\right] \] 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.black_litterman.bayesian import BlackLittermanEstimator
import pandas as pd

# Define views: "AAPL will outperform MSFT by 5%"
P = pd.DataFrame([[1, -1, 0]], columns=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"])
Q = pd.DataFrame([[0.05]])

bl = BlackLittermanEstimator(tau=0.05, risk_aversion=2.5)
mu_bl, cov_bl = bl.estimate(
    market_caps=market_caps,
    cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
    P=P,
    Q=Q,
)

Note

BlackLittermanEstimator is not a BaseReturnEstimator — it returns both (mu, cov) and is typically called directly or wrapped in a custom pipeline before the allocator step.

docs.title: Deep Learning / Foundation Models: TimesFM 3.0
docs.text:
Google's TimesFM 3.0 is a pretrained foundation model for zero-shot time-series forecasting. PyAlloq integrates TimesFM 3.0 for both point return estimation and probabilistic view generation for Black-Litterman.

Installation requirement

TimesFM integration requires the deep learning optional dependency: 

uv add pyalloq[dl]
# or pip install "pyalloq[dl]"

docs.title: Zero-Shot Return Estimation
docs.text:
PyAlloq provides both univariate and multivariate return estimators based on TimesFM 3.0:

  • TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts each asset series independently.
  • TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator: Forecasts cross-asset relationships jointly and optionally ingests past and future covariates from MarketData.features and MarketData.future_features.

For a forecast horizon \(H\) (in trading days) and forecasted price \(\hat{P}_{T+H, i}\), expected returns are annualized:

\[ \hat{\mu}_i = \left(\frac{\hat{P}_{T+H, i}}{P_{T, i}} - 1\right) \times \frac{252}{H} \] 
from pyalloq.dl.estimators.returns.timesfm import (
    TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator,
    TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator,
)
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

# Initialize the TimesFM 3.0 evaluator
tfm = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)

# 1. Univariate return estimator (forecasts assets independently)
univariate_est = TimesFM3UnivariateReturnEstimator(model=tfm, horizon=21)

# 2. Multivariate return estimator (leverages cross-asset dynamics & features)
multivariate_est = TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator(
    model=tfm, horizon=21, annualize=True
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=multivariate_est,
)

When to use: Zero-shot price forecasting across regimes without needing to train or fine-tune neural networks locally. Multivariate mode is ideal when macro/factor features or cross-asset dependencies exist.

docs.title: TimesFM 3.0 Black-Litterman View Generation
docs.text:
Black-Litterman typically requires subjective investor views (\(Q\)) and a diagonal confidence/uncertainty matrix (\(\Omega\)). TimesFM 3.0 natively outputs probabilistic forecast quantiles (\(p_{10}, p_{50}, p_{90}\)), which PyAlloq turns into objective, probabilistic views:

  1. View Vector (\(Q\)): The median forecast \(p_{50}\) defines the expected return view for each asset: [ Q_i = \left(\frac{p_{50, i}}{P_{T, i}} - 1\right) \times \frac{252}{H} ]
  2. Uncertainty Matrix (\(\Omega\)): Under a Gaussian assumption, the 80% credible interval (\(p_{10}\) to \(p_{90}\)) corresponds to \(2 \times 1.28 \approx 2.56\) standard deviations. The annualized forecast standard deviation is: [ \sigma_{i} = \frac{p_{90, i} - p_{10, i}}{2.56 \cdot P_{T, i}} \times \sqrt{\frac{252}{H}} ] The uncertainty matrix \(\Omega\) is the diagonal matrix of these view variances: [ \Omega = \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \ldots, \sigma_N^2\right) ]
  3. Picking Matrix (\(P\)): Identity matrix \(I_N\), since views are generated for all assets.
from pyalloq.dl.estimators.black_litterman.timesfm import (
    TimesFM3MultivariateViewGenerator,
    TimesFM3UnivariateViewGenerator,
)
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.black_litterman.bayesian import BlackLittermanEstimator
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

tfm = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)

# Generate objective views and uncertainty directly from TimesFM quantiles
view_generator = TimesFM3MultivariateViewGenerator(model=tfm, horizon=21)
P, Q, Omega = view_generator.generate(market_data)

# Blend with market equilibrium in Black-Litterman
bl = BlackLittermanEstimator(tau=0.05, risk_aversion=2.5)
mu_bl, cov_bl = bl.estimate(
    market_caps=market_data.cross_sectional,
    cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
    P=P,
    Q=Q,
)

When to use: You want Black-Litterman portfolio optimization but want systematic, probabilistic foundation model forecasts to drive the views and quantify view uncertainty.

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Return Estimator
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.interfaces import BaseReturnEstimator
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

class MyReturnEstimator(BaseReturnEstimator):
    def estimate(self, data: MarketData, **kwargs) -> pd.Series:
        # Annualized mean of log returns
        log_returns = data.prices.apply(lambda col: col.pct_change().add(1).apply(lambda x: x if x > 0 else 1e-6))
        return log_returns.mean() * 252

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=MyReturnEstimator(),
)

docs.title: Strategy Pipeline
docs.text: StrategyPipeline is the orchestrator that connects your return estimator, covariance estimator, and allocator into a single callable unit. It is the primary object consumed by WalkForwardEngine.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)
)

With defaults, StrategyPipeline uses:

  • Return estimator: EWMAReturnEstimator (60-day span)
  • Covariance estimator: EmpiricalCovariance

docs.title: Full Configuration
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(
        tickers=data.assets,
        objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE,
    ),
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
    allocator_kwargs={},  # optional extra kwargs forwarded to allocator.allocate()
)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When generate_weights(data) is called — either directly or by the backtest engine — it runs the following sequence:

def generate_weights(self, data: MarketData) -> pd.Series:
    expected_returns = self.returns_estimator.estimate(data)  # → pd.Series (N,)
    cov_matrix       = self.cov_estimator.estimate(data)      # → pd.DataFrame (N×N)

    result = self.allocator.allocate(
        data,
        cov_matrix=cov_matrix,
        expected_returns=expected_returns,
        **self.allocator_kwargs,
    )

    return result.weights  # → pd.Series (N,)

This means the pipeline is fully self-contained: given a MarketData slice, it produces portfolio weights.

docs.title: Using with WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
The pipeline is the only thing WalkForwardEngine needs to know about your strategy:

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline, rebalance_freq="ME")
results = engine.run(data)

The engine handles windowing, lookahead prevention, and cost accounting. The pipeline handles estimation and optimization.

docs.title: Calling Directly (Without Backtest)
docs.text:
You can also call the pipeline directly to get weights for a given data window, useful for live portfolio construction:

# Use the last 252 days
window_data = data.slice_time(end_date=data.prices.index[-1], lookback=252)
weights = pipeline.generate_weights(window_data)
print(weights)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description allocator BaseAllocator required The portfolio optimizer returns_estimator BaseReturnEstimator \| None EWMAReturnEstimator() Return estimator. Set to None to use default cov_estimator BaseCovarianceEstimator \| None EmpiricalCovariance() Covariance estimator. Set to None to use default allocator_kwargs dict {} Extra keyword arguments forwarded to allocator.allocate()

docs.title: Visualization & Tear Sheets (pyalloq-viz)
docs.text: pyalloq-viz provides an institutional visualization suite for pyalloq. It turns your optimization results, walk-forward backtests, Monte Carlo scenarios, and macroeconomic views into interactive Plotly figures and standalone HTML tear sheet dashboards.

docs.title: Architecture & Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["PyAlloq Engine Outputs"]
        MD["📦 MarketData &\nScenarioMarketData"]
        OPT["⚖️ OptimizationResult\n(Markowitz, HRP, RiskParity)"]
        BT["🔁 BacktestResult\nCPCVResult & PBOResult"]
        EP["🔭 EntropyResult &\nGMMRegimeGenerator"]
    end

    subgraph Viz["pyalloq-viz"]
        PLOTS["📈 Standalone Plot Functions\n(plot_fan_chart, plot_pbo_distribution, ...)"]
        TS["📋 TearSheet Builders\n(Simulation, Robustness, MacroRegime, Allocation)"]
    end

    subgraph Outputs["Deliverables"]
        FIG["🖥️ Interactive Plotly Figure\n(.to_figure() / .show())"]
        HTML["🌐 Standalone HTML Dashboard\n(.to_html('report.html'))"]
        IMG["🖼️ High-DPI Static Export\n(.save_image('report.png'))"]
    end

    Inputs --> PLOTS --> FIG
    Inputs --> TS
    TS --> FIG
    TS --> HTML
    TS --> IMG

docs.title: Two Ways to Visualize
docs.text:
1. Granular Plot Functions (plot_*): Every visualization is exposed as a standalone function returning a styled plotly.graph_objects.Figure.
  2. Composite Tear Sheet Classes (*TearSheet): Four specialized tear sheet classes group related charts and compute summary KPIs:
  3. SimulationTearSheet: Synthetic path cones, terminal wealth & ruin, CVaR tail shading, and drawdown cones.
  4. RobustnessTearSheet: Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) and Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) timeline scrambling.
  5. MacroRegimeTearSheet: Meucci Entropy Pooling prior-vs-posterior shifts and GMM Markov regime transition overlays.
  6. AllocationTearSheet: Multi-universe efficient frontier, weight drift & turnover, hierarchical treemaps, component risk contributions, and correlation/monthly return heatmaps.

docs.title: 1. The Multiverse & Simulation Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Evaluates synthetic futures (ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult), supporting both uniform scenario weights and view-adjusted posterior probabilities (EntropyResult).

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_fan_chart Median & expected equity trajectories enveloped by probability-weighted percentile bands (5–95, 10–90, 25–75) + spaghetti paths ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, optional EntropyResult, optional benchmark plot_terminal_wealth_ruin Terminal wealth density & histogram with shaded left-tail ruin region below 1 + ruin_threshold ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, ruin_threshold (e.g. -0.20) plot_cvar_tail_risk Return distribution with vertical markers at \(\text{VaR}_\alpha\) and \(\text{CVaR}_\alpha\) (Expected Shortfall) and shaded tail shortfall mass ScenarioMarketData, MonteCarloResult, or BacktestResult, alpha=0.05 plot_drawdown_fan_chart Underwater drawdown probability bands across all \(M\) synthetic trajectories ScenarioMarketData or MonteCarloResult, optional EntropyResult SimulationTearSheet Combines all 4 charts into a 2×2 figure or HTML dashboard with 7 summary KPIs All of the above TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq_simulation import GMMRegimeGenerator, ViewBuilder, AbsoluteView, EntropyPooler
from pyalloq_viz import SimulationTearSheet

# 1. Generate 500 synthetic paths over 63 trading days
gen = GMMRegimeGenerator(n_regimes=2, random_state=42)
gen.fit(market_data)
scenarios = gen.generate(n_paths=500, horizon=63)

# 2. Optional: Apply Entropy Pooling views
builder = ViewBuilder(scenarios)
A, b, C, d = builder.build([AbsoluteView(asset="AAPL", operator=">=", target=0.02)])
entropy_res = EntropyPooler(n_scenarios=scenarios.n_paths).fit(A_ineq=A, b_ineq=b, C_eq=C, d_eq=d)

# 3. Build & export the Simulation Tear Sheet
sim_ts = SimulationTearSheet(
    scenarios,
    asset_weights=backtest_result.weights.iloc[-1],
    entropy_result=entropy_res,
    ruin_threshold=-0.15,
    cvar_alpha=0.05,
    benchmark=backtest_result,
)

sim_ts.show()                              # Render 2x2 Plotly figure
sim_ts.to_html("simulation_report.html")   # Save standalone HTML dashboard

from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_fan_chart,
    plot_terminal_wealth_ruin,
    plot_cvar_tail_risk,
    plot_drawdown_fan_chart,
)

fig_fan  = plot_fan_chart(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, benchmark=backtest_result)
fig_ruin = plot_terminal_wealth_ruin(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, ruin_threshold=-0.15)
fig_cvar = plot_cvar_tail_risk(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res, alpha=0.05)
fig_dd   = plot_drawdown_fan_chart(scenarios, entropy_result=entropy_res)

docs.title: 2. Robustness & Overfitting Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Proves whether a strategy's historical performance is genuinely robust or an artifact of backtest overfitting and chronological luck, powered by PBOEvaluator and CPCVSplitter in pyalloq_backtest.

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_pbo_distribution CSCV Mode: Rank logit (\(\lambda_c\)) KDE with shaded overfitting mass (\(\lambda_c \le 0\)) + In-Sample vs. Out-of-Sample Sharpe degradation regression.Benchmark Mode: Simulated/CPCV Sharpe distribution vs. historical backtest Sharpe + survival ECDF. PBOResult, (T, M) trial matrix, or BacktestResult + CPCVResult/MonteCarloResult plot_cpcv_paths Recombined combinatorial timelines scrambling the chronological order of market regimes + path-level Sharpe vs. Max Drawdown scatter CPCVResult or BacktestResult RobustnessTearSheet Unified 2×2 overfitting & regime-scrambling dashboard with PBO, OOS loss probability, and CPCV survival KPIs BacktestResult, PBOResult, or (T, M) trial matrix Single-Strategy CPCV & Benchmark ModeMulti-Strategy CSCV Matrix Mode 
from pyalloq_backtest import CPCVSplitter
from pyalloq_viz import RobustnessTearSheet, plot_cpcv_paths, plot_pbo_distribution

# Scramble historical strategy returns across 6 chronological regime blocks
splitter = CPCVSplitter(n_groups=6, k_test_groups=2, max_paths=100)
cpcv_result = splitter.scramble_timelines(backtest_result)

# Individual plots:
fig_cpcv = plot_cpcv_paths(cpcv_result)
fig_pbo  = plot_pbo_distribution(backtest_result, synthetic_comparison=cpcv_result)

# Full Tear Sheet:
rob_ts = RobustnessTearSheet(backtest_result, cpcv_or_synthetic=cpcv_result)
rob_ts.to_html("robustness_report.html")

from pyalloq_backtest import PBOEvaluator
from pyalloq_viz import RobustnessTearSheet, plot_pbo_distribution

# Evaluate M candidate strategy configurations across S=8 combinatorial partitions
# strategy_trials_df has shape (T_days, M_trials)
pbo_eval = PBOEvaluator(n_partitions=8)
pbo_result = pbo_eval.evaluate_cscv(strategy_trials_df)

print(f"Probability of Backtest Overfitting: {pbo_result.pbo:.1%}")
fig = plot_pbo_distribution(pbo_result)

# Or generate the complete Tear Sheet directly from the (T, M) DataFrame:
RobustnessTearSheet(strategy_trials_df, n_partitions=8).to_html("cscv_pbo_report.html")

docs.title: 3. Macro Regime & Entropy Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Visualizes how subjective macroeconomic views warp the probability distribution of synthetic scenarios (EntropyPooler) and how portfolios behave across latent Gaussian Mixture Markov regimes (GMMRegimeGenerator).

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_entropy_pooling Left Panel: Uniform prior \(p_m = 1/M\) vs. sorted posterior \(x^*_m\) with KL Divergence and Effective Number of Scenarios (\(\text{ENS}\)).Right Panel: Prior vs. view-shifted posterior return density. EntropyResult, optional ScenarioMarketData plot_regime_transitions Historical Mode: Equity curve with dominant regime background shading + real-time posterior regime probabilities \(p_k(t)\).Synthetic Mode: Simulated equity cone + cross-sectional proportion of paths in each Markov state. BacktestResult or ScenarioMarketData, GMMRegimeGenerator MacroRegimeTearSheet Combines Entropy Pooling diagnostics and GMM regime transition overlays into a single report EntropyResult, BacktestResult or ScenarioMarketData, GMMRegimeGenerator TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq_viz import MacroRegimeTearSheet

macro_ts = MacroRegimeTearSheet(
    entropy_result=entropy_res,
    equity_or_scenarios=backtest_result,
    gmm_or_probs=gen,
    scenario_data=scenarios,
    market_data=market_data,
)
macro_ts.to_html("macro_regime_report.html")

from pyalloq_viz import plot_entropy_pooling, plot_regime_transitions

# 1. Entropy Pooling Prior vs. Posterior
fig_ep = plot_entropy_pooling(entropy_res, scenario_data=scenarios)

# 2. Historical Equity Curve with Decoded GMM Regime Shading
fig_hist_reg = plot_regime_transitions(
    backtest_result,
    gmm_or_probs=gen,
    market_data=market_data,
)

# 3. Synthetic Multiverse Markov State Proportions
fig_sim_reg = plot_regime_transitions(scenarios, gmm_or_probs=gen)

docs.title: 4. Allocation Mechanics & Risk Tear Sheet
docs.text:
Provides deep visibility into optimizer geometry, intra-rebalance weight drift, hierarchical clustering structure, risk parity budgets, and seasonal return patterns.

Function / Class What It Visualizes Key Inputs plot_multi_universe_frontier Parametric Markowitz frontier + random Dirichlet portfolio cloud + optimal allocations solved across synthetic scenarios expected_returns, cov_matrix, optional scenario_data & allocator_or_pipeline plot_weight_drift_turnover Reconstructs daily intra-rebalance drifted weights (sawtooth drift + rebalance snap-backs) and two-way rebalance turnover bars BacktestResult, MarketData plot_hierarchical_composition Multi-level Treemap (Portfolio -> Sector/Cluster -> Asset) + Current vs. Target/Benchmark horizontal bar chart OptimizationResult or pd.Series, optional target_or_benchmark_weights, MarketData plot_risk_contributions Capital weights (\(w_i\)) vs. Percentage Component Risk Contributions (\(\text{PCRC}_i\)) vs. Target Risk Budgets (\(b_i\)) OptimizationResult or pd.Series, cov_matrix plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns Quasi-diagonalized asset correlation heatmap + Year × Month (Jan–Dec) periodic return heatmap with annual totals MarketData or cov_matrix, BacktestResult AllocationTearSheet Combines allocation, risk parity, drift, and correlation diagnostics into a unified report All of the above TearSheet DashboardIndividual Plot Functions 
from pyalloq.ml.optimizers.hrp import HRPAllocator
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_budgeting import RiskBudgetingAllocator
from pyalloq_viz import AllocationTearSheet

cov = market_data.get_returns().cov() * 252.0
mu  = market_data.get_returns().mean() * 252.0

hrp = HRPAllocator(tickers=market_data.assets)
hrp_res = hrp.allocate(market_data, cov_matrix=cov)
rb_res  = RiskBudgetingAllocator(tickers=market_data.assets).allocate(market_data, cov_matrix=cov)

alloc_ts = AllocationTearSheet(
    optimization_result=hrp_res,
    backtest_result=backtest_result,
    market_data=market_data,
    cov_matrix=cov,
    expected_returns=mu,
    scenario_data=scenarios,
    allocator_or_pipeline=hrp,
    target_weights=rb_res,
)
alloc_ts.to_html("allocation_report.html")

from pyalloq_viz import (
    plot_multi_universe_frontier,
    plot_weight_drift_turnover,
    plot_hierarchical_composition,
    plot_risk_contributions,
    plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns,
)

fig_ef   = plot_multi_universe_frontier(mu, cov, scenario_data=scenarios, allocator_or_pipeline=hrp, optimal_portfolios=[hrp_res, rb_res])
fig_wd   = plot_weight_drift_turnover(backtest_result, market_data=market_data)
fig_tree = plot_hierarchical_composition(hrp_res, target_or_benchmark_weights=rb_res, market_data=market_data)
fig_rc   = plot_risk_contributions(rb_res, cov_matrix=cov)
fig_corr = plot_correlation_and_periodic_returns(market_data, portfolio_returns=backtest_result)

docs.title: Themes & Static Exports
docs.text:
Every plot function and tear sheet supports two built-in institutional themes:

  • "alloq_dark" (default): Slate/obsidian background (#0B0F19) with high-contrast emerald, cyan, amber, coral, crimson, and violet semantic accents.
  • "alloq_light": Clean publication white/slate background (#FFFFFF) tailored for PDFs and print reports.
from pyalloq_viz import plot_fan_chart, apply_plotly_theme

# Pass theme directly to any plot function or TearSheet method
fig = plot_fan_chart(scenarios, theme="alloq_light")

# Or re-style an existing Plotly or Matplotlib figure
apply_plotly_theme(fig, theme="alloq_dark", title="Custom Title", subtitle="Custom Subtitle")
